sections.content:
From my understanding, this course seems to be split into two parts, one business/macro view, and one individual view.

**Business view**

Don't ask me what I learned, because I have absolutely no clue for this part. There isn't a clear logical structure, just scattered pieces of information that somehow we have to integrate into something coherent. But maybe that's just my science/math brain thinking this way. Maybe you prefer this structure. It's up to you.

Here's a rough keyword syllabus of what I can kind of recall. Note that this is not exhaustive because my memory is fuzzy:
1. Shareholder and stakeholder theory
2. Five types of power, power-interest matrix
3. Transparency and accountability
4. McNamara Fallacy, Goodhart's Law, Partisan Law
5. Apologies and crisis communication
6. Diversity policies, gentrification

**Individual view**

Now this. This part is my highlight of the course, especially when combined with Prof Brown's delivery. Way more practical and insightful than the business stuff, and it gets kind of philosophical at times. It made me reflect on myself after the lecture, which is super rare. Amazing job Prof Brown.

Keyword syllabus again:
1. Personal and community values
2. Happiness (What makes us happy?)
3. Team/Community dynamics and behaviour, psychological safety

Still giving a C for an unorganized structure though.
sections.teaching:
Prof Brown is probably the best professor/teacher I have encountered in my UST life so far. He's energetic, engaging and enthusiastic, and he has a clear passion for teaching. Despite the course's messy structure, he tries to incorporate storytelling and tie things together. You feel as though you have just experienced a TED talk, a well-made  a motivational workshop, letting ideas sink in, and adding plot twists, surprises and jokes. That's why I'm able to reflect on his lectures and absorb his ideas. Given the course's uninspiring content, he managed to make it bearable, layman-friendly and sometimes inspiring, something that I feel like every teacher/teaching professor should strive to achieve.

For participation, he tries to give everyone a chance to speak up and earn participation points, encouraging those who haven't spoken to answer questions at times, and you can sign up for optional reading summaries to earn participation points if you're afraid to raise your hand.

Best still, he cares about his students. He gives us a chance to seriously think about our values, how we would want to prioritize when faced with tradeoffs, and what we want to do in our future lives. He gives you the opportunity to receive his guidance (but I doubt that many people would make use of this), so if you are serious about your career, he is always happy to help.

A true S-tier prof in this economy and in this uni? Such a rare gem. That's why even though his grades might not be that good, I still highly recommend taking his lecture sections. I took away something way better and way more worthwhile than two letters and a number on my transcript.

Your group needs to take a problem-solving approach and answer the following questions regarding the firm. 1) What are the social and environmental challenges to the firm’s industry? 2) Has the firm taken any measures to address the issues? 3) How may the firm further improve based on your suggestions? sections.content:
Really good content. Nowadays a lot of companies keep bragging about CSR, but is it really CSR, or is it just public relation tools? The course will take a look at how real companies handle CSR issues such as long-term corporate strategies, handling corporate scandals, ethical decision making, etc. You also get to know the dark side of the story - how CSR was initially taken in a shallow approach, and how companies like Link REIT can bullsh!t and brag about 'Shared Value'. Overall a really good course that will stimulate our thinking.

I don't know why some students think ethics courses are useless. Believe me - you'll be shocked at how many students don't even know it's illegal for a ship captain not to exercise prudent seamanship. I think every one of us should treat this course seriously - professionalism is one of the key aspects companies value a lot. Don't take a very ignorant view on professionalism.

sections.content:
This intermediate business ethics course takes a discussion-based approach to examining ethical issues in a corporate context. This course focuses on the ethical issues related to the interaction between business and society. You will further develop your knowledge, moral reasoning skills, and attitudes towards social responsibility by considering the perspectives of various stakeholders. Corporate contexts sometimes involve ‘managerial mischief’ and ‘moral mazes’; thus having an awareness and sensitivity to Business Ethics can bring overall improvements. This highly interactive course will draw upon relevant current issues to help you understand (and overcome)
some of the real-world challenges that business executives confront. Ultimately, this course will encourage you to become positive, ethical influences in your own personal and professional lives.

From my point of view, the content of this course is quite interesting as it explores us the complex business ethical issue nowadays which is useful to develop our "water-blowing" skills in future.
sections.teaching:

5th: another pair discussion on some ethical decision topics
6th: group discussion/group work (according to your group)

sections.content: In terms of content, I found it quite similar to SBMT2010 as it was mainly based on ethics and being ethical. However it is less vague, and there are many instances where ethics is applied to real life situations and ourselves.
sections.teaching: Although it was a 9am lesson, most students were able to attend the classes on time. Melody made all the classes very interesting, she would make jokes and also engage all students. I had a lot of fun attending her lessons, and did not find waking up for 9am lessons difficult at all. Overall, the teaching was very good.
sections.grading:
Your grade is mainly based on how much you participate in class. Melody marks down your name if you do speak up in class (as everyone has to put their name card on their desk every lesson). I think that it is crucial you attend all lessons as there are only 13 lessons and participation is HEAVILY depended on.

There is also another essay and project which you have to do. The essay is a reflection journal on how you felt about the classes and what you learnt, which I don't think matters a lot to your grade as long as you hand it in on time. As for the project, I do think it is quite important and you must think on a deeper level to show that you have really put effort into the project. Also, most people made really professional presentations, so the presentation aspect is really important as well.
sections.workload:
For those who rather do projects than take exams, you won't find that the workload is large. You would have to meet up a lot with your group mates to make sure that the project is completed. The project does require you to think deeply (not just on a superficial level), which I thought was quite good.

But many of my classmates complained that for a 2 credit course the workload is too much (which I do agree to an extent)
